title: Bone & Oxblood — The Literary Essay Folio
description: A type-only opener in the tradition of The Drift and n+1: an asymmetric transitional serif title anchored to the upper-left third, an author name set modestly beneath, and a hairline Roman numeral claiming the opposite corner. No imagery competes — proportion and weight do all the work.
philosophy: This template rejects every convention that mistakes decoration for meaning. It exists for writing that trusts itself — the kind published in journals that run no advertisements and are read aloud before they are projected. Asymmetry produces intellectual tension without spectacle; the oxblood numeral is the sole concession to ornament. The speaker who reaches for this layout already knows the words are carrying the room.
goodFor: Essay or long-form talk opener slides at literary conferences
Single-author readings, book launches, and chapbook presentations
Humanities thesis or dissertation defense title slides
Academic lecture series where the argument precedes any visual
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews requiring dense data hierarchy
Product launch decks built around hero photography or video stills
Multi-speaker panel title slides needing visual differentiation per speaker
Sales decks where brand color compliance overrides typographic restraint
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide reads like the opening folio of a respected literary journal — spare, self-assured, and unapologetically typographic. Asymmetric tension arises between the weighted title mass anchored at upper-left and the hair-thin numeral claiming the far corner, with vast negative space between them signaling intellectual seriousness rather than emptiness. Mood is austere without coldness: a warm, parchment-like stillness punctuated by a single precise ornamental note in deep oxblood. Avoid anything decorative, pictorial, centered, or symmetry-seeking — drama is earned through restraint alone.

examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid with an ~8% outer margin on all sides; title text anchors flush-left in the upper third, spanning roughly the left seven columns and sitting high in the top quarter of the vertical field. Author name runs beneath the title in the same left-aligned column band at a significantly reduced scale — hierarchy established through size contrast alone, no rule lines or weight shifts needed. The lower-right corner is claimed by a lone hairline Roman numeral set in the oxblood accent, isolated as a structural counterweight with no surrounding elements. No header band, no footer bar, no imagery — the remaining field is intentional negative space.

examples.promptCore: The slide reads like a page lifted from a literary quarterly — austere, unhurried, trusting the prose to do all persuasive work. A single dense text block pulls leftward while the empty right margin acts as intellectual counterweight rather than wasted space; the oxblood numeral is the sole ornamental concession, anchoring without decorating. Asymmetric tension is produced entirely through proportion and weight contrast, not through color fields or graphic devices. Avoid icons, tonal banding, rule clusters, or anything that competes with the argument on the page.

<svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 1920 1080" preserveAspectRatio="xMidYMid meet">
  <rect width="1920" height="1080" fill="#f5f0e6"/>

  <!-- Running header -->
  <g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a">
    <text x="140" y="118" font-size="16" letter-spacing="6" font-style="italic" fill="#7a7468">The Bone & Oxblood Folio  ·  Spring Quarterly  ·  Vol. XII</text>
    <text x="1780" y="118" font-size="16" letter-spacing="4" text-anchor="end" fill="#7a7468">ESSAY  III  —  ON ATTENTION</text>
  </g>

  <!-- Hairline rule -->
  <line x1="140" y1="148" x2="1780" y2="148" stroke="#1e1c1a" stroke-width="1"/>

  <!-- Oxblood section numeral (right margin, cols 9–12) -->
  <g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#7d2a2a">
    <text x="1780" y="520" font-size="360" font-weight="400" font-style="italic" text-anchor="end" letter-spacing="-8">III</text>
  </g>

  <!-- Primary text block (cols 1–8) -->
  <g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a">
    <!-- Kicker -->
    <text x="140" y="300" font-size="18" letter-spacing="8" fill="#7a7468">§  THESIS</text>

    <!-- Thesis — long pull-quote -->
    <text x="140" y="378" font-size="54" font-style="italic" font-weight="400">
      <tspan x="140" dy="0">“ To read slowly is not a nostalgia but a</tspan>
      <tspan x="140" dy="72">discipline; the sentence that resists us</tspan>
      <tspan x="140" dy="72">is the one that most deserves our</tspan>
      <tspan x="140" dy="72">patience, and, in returning, our trust. ”</tspan>
    </text>

    <!-- Attribution -->
    <text x="140" y="732" font-size="20" letter-spacing="4" fill="#7a7468">— HELENA VOSS,  <tspan font-style="italic">Against the Scroll</tspan>  (2024)</text>

    <!-- Short prose continuation -->
    <g font-size="22" font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a">
      <text x="140" y="820">
        <tspan x="140" dy="0">Voss’s claim, rehearsed throughout the essay, is not that difficulty is a virtue in itself, but that</tspan>
        <tspan x="140" dy="34">attention is a moral practice — a willingness to remain with what does not immediately yield.</tspan>
        <tspan x="140" dy="34">The argument of these pages is narrower, and perhaps more modest: that criticism begins only</tspan>
        <tspan x="140" dy="34">after the first reading has failed us, and that the second reading is where literature is kept.</tspan>
      </text>
    </g>
  </g>

  <!-- Folio / page indicator, flush-right baseline -->
  <g font-family="Georgia, ui-serif, serif" fill="#1e1c1a">
    <line x1="1700" y1="990" x2="1780" y2="990" stroke="#1e1c1a" stroke-width="0.75"/>
    <text x="1780" y="1020" font-size="18" letter-spacing="3" text-anchor="end">FOLIO  ·  047</text>
  </g>

  <!-- Subtle left folio mark -->
  <text x="140" y="1020" font-family="ui-monospace, monospace" font-size="13" letter-spacing="3" fill="#7a7468">BV.XII / SPRING / MMXXVI</text>
</svg>
examples.layoutNotes: 12-column grid; the primary text block — a thesis, a set of numbered propositions, or a long pull-quote with modest attribution below — occupies cols 1–8 with a generous top margin that lets the argument gather before it begins. A full-width hairline rule separates a minimal running header (essay title or section label) from the body below. Cols 9–12 form a deliberately spare right-hand margin reserved for a single oxblood section numeral or a brief marginal gloss, never both simultaneously. Folio number sits flush-right at the baseline.
